comments.story_title: Refactoring: How do I even start?
comments.why_zh: 重构 OOP 代码：先增加结构，再整合收拢
comments.quote_zh: 对理解 OOP 代码重构的整体概念来说非常精彩。
comments.text_zh: Sandi Metz 的演讲《All the Little Things》[0] 对理解 OOP 代码重构的整体概念来说非常精彩。它以 Ruby 为中心，但这些概念适用于所有 OOP 语言。最有意思的一点是：在重构过程中，你其实应该先增加代码量和复杂度，最终再把它们整合、聚拢下来。这与单纯尝试删除/改动代码的做法正好相反。[0] - [VIDEO]
comments.text: Sandi Metz talk "All the Little Things"[0] is amazing for understanding the general concepts around refactoring OOP code. It's ruby centric, but the concepts are applicable to all OOP languages. The most interesting part is the fact that during the refactoring process you should actually increase the amount of code and complexity to eventually consolidate and aggregate it down. This as opposed to simply trying to delete/mutate code. [0] - [VIDEO]

comments.author: tinco
comments.story_title: Talks that changed the way I think about programming
comments.why_zh: 具体例子让编程风格不再只靠直觉
comments.quote_zh: 这个演讲用一个例子囊括了所有重要价值。
comments.text_zh: 这些演讲有点偏向游戏/高性能编程这一侧，但总体仍然非常有意思。在我已经看过的那些里，我特别喜欢 Mike Acton 的演讲。既然这个帖子已经变得这么好，我想补充几个：* Sandi Metz 讲解 Gilded Rose 或《All the small things》[VIDEO] 我已经认同她的编程风格以及广义上的 Ruby TDD/BDD 运动，但这个演讲用一个例子囊括了所有重要价值。我觉得它让我的编程风格不再建立在经验或直觉这类模糊的东西上，而是建立在这次演讲所展示的具体优点上。* Matthew Brecknell 演示 Hole Driven Development [LINK] 这个视频里展示的编程风格真的让人脑洞大开。我觉得大多数 Haskell 程序员用的是它的弱化版，Matthew 把它推到了极致。我没有采用这种风格，我不觉得它实用，但这类东西总有一天会被某个人以更舒服的方式融入新语言或平台，成为一项革命性特性。
comments.text: These talks are a little skewed to the game/high performance programming side of the art, but still very interesting in general. Of the ones I've already seen I really like Mike Acton's talk. Since this has become such a nice thread some additions I'd add: * Sandi Metz going through the Gilded Rose or "All the small things" [VIDEO] I already subscribed to her programming style and the general Ruby TDD/BDD movement, but this talk captures all the important values in a single example. I think it made my programming style no longer based on vague things like experience or intuition, but just on concrete merit shown in this talk. * Matthew Brecknell demonstrating Hole Driven Development [LINK] The programming style demonstrated in this video is a real mind bender. I think most Haskell programmers use a weaker version of this, Matthew takes it to the extreme. I didn't adapt this style, I don't think it's practical, but it's the sort of thing that some person someday will incorporate in some more comfortable way in a new language or platform as a revolutionary feature.

comments.text: I'm a huge proponent of this concept. The goal is to be able to build and iterate as fast as possible. Needless abstraction slows this down and makes the app more brittle to changes in response to customer/client inputs. Sandi Metz had an awesome presentation about this during a Rails Conf. "Duplication is far cheaper than wrong abstraction" [VIDEO] Her blog talking more about the assertion: [LINK]

comments.text_zh: 这条讨论让我想起 Sandi Metz 的一句很棒的引言，她在 ruby 社区里以反复强调这个话题而相当有名。她在一次演讲里说过的、让我印象特别深的一点是：重复优于错误的抽象。新程序员最先被灌输的就是 DRY。它容易理解，效果也还算不错。再进一步，似乎就是要知道什么时候_不该_把东西归并起来，以及如何判断你看到的是一段需要具体化为独立实体或函数的独立逻辑。补充：我提到的那场 Sandi Metz 演讲：[VIDEO]
comments.text: This line of discussion reminds me of a great quote by Sandi Metz, who's pretty well known in the ruby community for harping on the topic. One thing I saw in a talk of hers that really stuck with me: Repetition is preferable to the wrong abstraction. The first thing that's drilled into a new programmer is DRY. It's easy to understand and it works reasonably well. The next step up seems to be knowing when _not_ to roll stuff up, and how to tell when you're looking at a distinct piece of logic that needs to be reified into it's own entity or function. comments.author: voodootrucker
comments.story_title: Admitting That Functional Programming Can Be Awkward (2007)
comments.why_zh: 解释如何避免错误的抽象，让架构自然浮现
comments.quote_zh: Sandi Metz 说得比我好得多
comments.text_zh: 在教 OOP 时，我 _真的_ 很努力地避免使用人为编造的例子。这非常难，因为直到你的应用变得不再简单，你才真正需要它，所以我能理解为什么大学课程都用汽车和卡车之类的例子。我想我最后选的是带磁带、唱片、CD 等的 Player API。有些可以跳过，另一些只能快进。我仍然对它不满意，但它比大多数例子都好。我喜欢建议大家去写一个 IntelliJ 插件。我发现一些架构最好的 OOP 程序最终不过是一堆插件接口和基类的集合。但你真的需要理解“is a”与“has a”的区别，不要烧掉你的基类，让架构遵循 rule of 3 自然浮现，而不是匆忙跳上错误的抽象去对抗重复。Sandi Metz 说得比我好得多：[VIDEO]
comments.text: I _really_ struggled to not use contrived examples when teaching OOP. It was very hard because you don't really need it until your application becomes non-trivial so I see why all the college classes use cars & trucks or whatever. I think I ended up going with a Player API with tapes, records, CDs etc. Some could skip, others only fast-forward. I was still unhappy with it, but it was better than most examples. I like to point folks at writing an IntelliJ plugin. I find that some of the best architected OOP programs become nothing but a collection of plugin interfaces and base classes. But you really need to understand "is a" vs "has a", not burn your base class, let architecture emerge following the rule of 3, rather than quickly jumping on the wrong abstraction to fight duplication. Sandi Metz really says it better than I can: [VIDEO]

comments.author: unscaled
comments.story_title: The Wrong Abstraction (2016)
comments.why_zh: 原始演讲主张保留重复并等待正确的抽象
comments.quote_zh: 文章链接的那场 2014 年原始演讲[1]说得很清楚：_保留重复_
comments.text_zh: 我（也）想这样理解这篇文章，但我觉得文章在这一点上有点含糊。它聚焦于 Programmer X，也就是在多次尝试把功能硬塞进一个非常错误的抽象之后才接手的人。文章同意这个抽象在 Programmer A 写它的时候是有用的，但对于 Programmer A 的判断在第 2 步或第 3 步时是否正确，仍然含糊其辞！我不太确定 Sandi Metz 现在是怎么想的，但文章链接的那场 2014 年原始演讲[1]说得很清楚：_保留重复_，并_等待正确的抽象_。这个说法听起来更符合 Rule of Three，或者 Go 谚语 'a little copying is better than a little dependency'，也就是这里人们争论的点。就我个人而言，我认为任何非平凡的重复都应该在第一时间消除，以避免意外的业务逻辑分歧。我觉得后一种情况比不得不处理错误抽象风险更大，因为——正如 Sandi 在这里雄辩地解释的那样——错误的抽象可以（而且应该！）被重构。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: I also (want to) understand the article this way, but I think the article is a bit vague about this point. It focuses on Programmer X, who is coming after many iterations of trying to retrofit features into a very wrong abstraction. The article agrees that the abstraction was useful when Programmer A wrote it, but it remains vague about whether Programmer A's judgement was correct at step 2 or 3! I'm not quite sure what Sandi Metz is thinking right now, but the original 2014 talk[1] linked in the article is pretty clear about _keeping the duplication_, and _waiting for the right abstraction_. This statement sounds more in line with the Rule of Three, or the Go proverb 'a little copying is better than a little dependency', which is what people are arguing here. Personally, I believe that any non-trivial duplication should be eliminated at the very first chance, to avoid unintended business logic divergence. I find the later case more risky than having to deal with the wrong abstraction, since - as Sandi eloquently explains here - wrong abstractions can (and should!) be refactored. [1] [VIDEO]

comments.story_title: Factory Factory Factory
comments.text_zh: 强烈同意。对我来说，一个有用框架的标志是它能降低你所要完成任务复杂度。如果它增加了任务复杂度，那它就不是适合这项工作的工具！选择合适的抽象层级是软件工程中最重要的部分。如果你只需要 HTTP 路由，那 Flask 很棒，但每次我尝试用它来做 Django 擅长的事情（数据库、模板、表单）时，我都不得不实际上自己滚出一个糟糕的 Django 版本。（类似那句：每个足够大的 C++ 程序里都嵌着一个实现得很糟糕的 LISP。）我曾见过一个巨大的 Flask 安装极其戏剧性地展示了这一点，它本可以从施加一点结构约束中大大受益。我在看到代码后很快就离开了那份工作，因为理解那些设计糟糕的抽象会是一件极其痛苦的事。但这甚至不是维护者的错——代码相当不错，但抽象和业务逻辑都只由一个人设计。而抽象之所以有泄漏，只是因为抽象本身就很难设计。框架让你可以把框架之下的架构决策完全卸载到许多人年的设计、bug 修复和安全修复上。我如何给请求添加头部？Django 有一种有主见的方式。我把数据库模型放在哪里？models.py，而且如果你放在那里，你就不需要做任何 c
comments.text: Strongly agree. For me the mark of a useful framework is that is reduces the complexity of the task you are trying to do. If it increases the complexity of the task, it isn't the right tool for the job! Choosing the right level of abstraction is the most important part of software engineering. If all you need is HTTP routing, then Flask is great, but every time I tried to use it for the kinds of things Django is great at (databasing, templating, forms), I had to effectively roll my own crappy version of Django. (Something something every sufficiently large C++ program has a poorly implemented version of LISP embedded into it.) I saw this dramatically demonstrated by an enormous Flask installation that would have greatly benefited from a little imposed structure. I bounced hard from that gig after being shown the code because it was going to be a massive pain to understand the poorly designed abstractions. But it wasn't even the maintainer's fault - it was pretty good code but it had only been designed by one person, both the abstractions and the business logic. And the abstractions were leaky simply because abstractions are difficult to design. The framework allows you to completely offload the architectural decisions underneath the framework to many person-years worth of design, bug squashing, and security fixes. How do I add headers to a request? Django has one opinionated way. Where do I put my database models? models.py and if you put them there you don't have to do any c

comments.text_zh: 从个人经验来看，性别差异可能让人感到畏惧，但一旦你开始在行业中建立人脉并获得更多经验，就会变得容易。在我做实习生的时候，我最初的几位导师就是女性软件工程师，她们技术能力出众，对团队不可或缺。很多大学都有女性科技俱乐部，你可以在那里结识其他女性并接受她们的指导，许多科技公司也非常重视从包括女性在内的代表性不足群体中招聘和留住优秀人才。至于值得敬仰的女性，我没有一份详尽的名单，但以下是想到的几位：- Sandi Metz：[VIDEO] - Melanie Perkins，Canva 联合创始人 - Ella Ehrlich：[LINK] 另外，YC 保留了一份由女性创立的公司名单（比你想象的多得多）：[LINK]
comments.text: From personal experience, the gender disparity can feel daunting but it gets easier once you start building your network in the industry and getting more experience. In my days as an intern, some of my first mentors were women software engineers with exceptional technical abilities who were indispensable to their teams. Lots of colleges have clubs for women in tech where you can meet and be mentored by other women, and many tech companies have placed a heavy focus on hiring and retaining strong talent from underrepresented groups including women. As for women to look up to, I don't have an exhaustive list but here are a few that come to mind: - Sandi Metz: [VIDEO] - Melanie Perkins, co-founder of Canva - Ella Ehrlich: [LINK] Also, YC keeps a list of all of their women-founded companies (there are a lot more than you might expect): [LINK]
